summary: Degarelix is a GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) receptor antagonist used as androgen-deprivation therapy for advanced prostate cancer. By directly and reversibly blocking pituitary GnRH receptors it rapidly suppresses luteinising hormone and testosterone WITHOUT the initial testosterone surge (flare) seen with GnRH agonists, so no antiandrogen flare cover is needed. It is given as a subcutaneous depot - a 240 mg loading dose then 80 mg every 28 days - and commonly causes injection-site reactions, hot flushes and the metabolic/cardiovascular consequences of low testosterone.
indications: Treatment of patients with advanced prostate cancer (androgen-deprivation therapy)

dosage.d: 240 mg given as two subcutaneous injections of 120 mg each (40 mg/mL)

dosage.n: First maintenance dose 28 days after the starting dose

admin: For subcutaneous use in the abdominal region ONLY - reconstitute and inject as a depot
Give starting dose as two separate 120 mg injections; rotate injection sites and avoid areas exposed to pressure (waistband, ribs)
Administer maintenance 80 mg every 28 days; a window of a few days is generally acceptable
Reconstitute strictly per product instructions and inject promptly as a slow deep SC injection
moa: Degarelix binds reversibly to pituitary GnRH receptors as an antagonist, immediately reducing the release of luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone and thereby rapidly lowering testosterone to castrate levels. Because it blocks (rather than initially stimulates) the receptor, it avoids the testosterone surge and clinical flare associated with GnRH agonists.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to degarelix or any component
relative: Congenital long QT syndrome or risk of QT prolongation
Severe hepatic or renal impairment (not studied)

preg: Not indicated in women. Degarelix is contraindicated in pregnancy; based on mechanism and animal data it could cause fetal harm.
lact: Not indicated in women and therefore not relevant to breastfeeding.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed in mild to moderate renal impairment. Degarelix has not been adequately studied in severe renal impairment - use with caution and monitor.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed in mild to moderate hepatic impairment, though exposure may be modestly reduced; it has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment, so monitor liver function and testosterone suppression.

major: Class IA and class III antiarrhythmics and other QT-prolonging drugs (additive QT prolongation - combination should be considered carefully)
moderate: Drugs causing electrolyte disturbance e.g. diuretics (worsen QT risk)
minor: No significant CYP-mediated interactions expected (peptide, not CYP metabolised)
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses serum testosterone and lowers PSA (markers of response); may prolong QT and elevate liver transaminases

common: Injection-site reactions (pain, erythema, swelling, induration, nodule)
serious: Long-term: decreased bone mineral density / fractures
Metabolic effects - hyperglycaemia/new diabetes and cardiovascular events
Erectile dysfunction and loss of libido

monitoring: Serum testosterone (to confirm castrate level) and PSA
ECG/QT and serum electrolytes, especially with cardiac risk
Bone mineral density during long-term therapy
counsel: This injection is given under the skin of the abdomen, usually every 28 days - keep your appointments
The injection site may be sore, red or lumpy for a while; rotate sites
Expect hot flushes, reduced sex drive and possible weight gain from low testosterone
Tell your doctor about any heart rhythm problems or fainting
Long-term treatment can weaken bones and affect blood sugar - your doctor will monitor these
pk: Testosterone falls to castrate levels within about 3 days in most patients
Peak plasma concentration approximately 2 days after the depot injection
Depot maintains castrate testosterone over the 28-day dosing interval
Store the vials at room temperature 20-25 C; reconstitute immediately before use
pearls: Unlike GnRH agonists, degarelix produces NO initial testosterone flare, so no antiandrogen cover is required at initiation
Achieves castrate testosterone faster than agonists - useful when rapid suppression is desirable (e.g. high tumour burden, cord-compression risk)
Injection-site reactions are the most frequent adverse effect, mainly after the loading dose; rotate abdominal sites
Monitor QT interval in patients with cardiac risk or on other QT-prolonging drugs
Long-term androgen deprivation carries bone, metabolic and cardiovascular risks - monitor and manage proactively
missed: Maintenance doses are given every 28 days by a clinician. If a dose is delayed, it should be given as soon as possible; a substantial delay may allow testosterone to rise, so contact the clinic promptly to reschedule. Do not attempt to self-administer.
overdose: There is no clinical experience with acute overdose. Because effects relate to androgen suppression and possible QT prolongation, management is supportive with cardiac and clinical monitoring; degarelix is not dialysable to a useful degree. There is no specific antidote.
